reality: TANK/PLATOON COMMS, 1942-45 (what actually happened): Every German tank carried a Funkgerät (Fu/FuG). The standard fit was **Fu 5** (10 W.S.c transmitter + Ukw.E.e receiver, 27.0–33.3 MHz, 125 channels at 50 kHz spacing, 2 m rod antenna) — voice (AM) range roughly 2–4 km moving (a 1942 US intelligence report on the Pz IV gives ~3.75 mi voice / ~6.25 mi CW), Morse/CW roughly 4–10 km. Ordinary tanks in a platoon often had only **Fu 2** (receiver only!) — they could HEAR the platoon leader but not reply by radio; the platoon/company leaders' tanks had the full Fu 5 transceiver. Tiger I: Fu 5 in the hull under the glacis, operated by the dedicated fifth crewman (Funker, who also manned the bow MG); Fu 2 additionally in platoon-leader vehicles. Command tanks (Panzerbefehlswagen, Befehlstiger) carried long-range **Fu 7** (ground-air liaison) or **Fu 8** (30 W medium-wave, frame/star antenna, ~10 km voice / tens of km CW) to talk to regiment/division. PROCEDURE: within a platoon (3-4 Tigers, spacing ~100 m) traffic was plain-voice, terse, over throat microphones (Kehlkopfmikrofon) and headsets, using daily-changed callsigns from the German spelling alphabet (Anton, Berta, Cäsar, Dora...), map-grid Planquadrat references, and clock-direction target calls. Flags, hand signals, and flare pistols backed up the radio at platoon level. ENIGMA'S REAL PLACE: Enigma I lived at **regiment, division, corps and higher HQs** — in signal-battalion radio trucks and command posts, operated by trained Funker pairs (one on the machine, one on the Morse key), never inside a gun tank. A Tiger platoon leader would never touch one; his encrypted link to higher command was via the company/battalion net, and anything Enigma-enciphered was keyed out in Morse by the staff radio section. Tactical tank traffic was too time-critical for machine cipher — it was protected only by brevity, callsigns, and low VHF range. So the game's premise inverts reality on exactly one axis: real platoon command was instant insecure voice; Enigma was slow, secure, and two echelons up.
machine_details: ENIGMA I (Wehrmacht 3-rotor "Services Enigma") — Blender/UI reference: OVERALL: oak wooden case ~28 × 34 × 15 cm closed, ~12 kg; hinged lid (often with a spare-bulb rack and the Steckerbrett cable clips inside the lid), leather carry strap or metal handle; black wrinkle-finish metal inner chassis. LAYOUT top-to-bottom as the operator sees it: (1) three **rotor thumb-wheels** protruding through slots in the lid plate, each beside a small **glass window** showing one letter of the rotor ring (A–Z on Heer machines; some rings numbered 01–26); rotors chosen 3-from-5 (I–V) daily per the Schlüsseltafel key sheet, each with a settable ring (Ringstellung) and one turnover notch; leftmost is the fixed reflector (UKW-B). (2) **Lampboard**: 26 glow-lamps under letter stencils in three rows, QWERTZ order — row1 QWERTZUIO, row2 ASDFGHJK, row3 PYXCVBNML — plus two test sockets. (3) **Keyboard**: 26 round keys, same QWERTZ rows; no numbers, no space, no umlauts (numbers spelled out or via substitution; CH→Q; X used as space/stop). (4) Front face behind a fold-down flap: the **Steckerbrett plugboard**, 26 double-jack sockets in QWERTZ rows; 10 twin-plug cables swap letter pairs (12 cables supplied, 2 spares in the lid). POWER: 4.5 V Wehrmacht flat battery in a side compartment with hinged lid, or external 4 V via screw terminals; a brightness/battery selector switch. OPERATION SEQUENCE (this is your diegetic UI loop): set the day key (rotor order, Ringstellung, plug pairs) → turn thumb-wheels to a start position → type a 3-letter message key twice-enciphered (early war) or per 1940+ procedure once, reset wheels to the chosen key → press one key per plaintext letter with the LEFT hand while writing down whichever lamp lights with the RIGHT — the machine has NO printer and NO transmitter → hand the ciphertext, chopped into 5-letter groups with a preamble (callsigns, time, group count, Kenngruppe), to the Morse operator, who keys it out on a separate transmitter. Rightmost rotor steps once per keypress (audible ratchet clack), with occasional double-step of the middle rotor. Enciphering is symmetric: same setup deciphers. Speed: a good two-man team managed only a few characters per second end-to-end — messages were minutes, not moments.
liberties: Cleanest framing, in ascending order of elegance — recommend the last: (a) BEFEHLSTIGER HANDWAVE: the player's Tiger is a one-off command conversion (real Befehlstiger existed, with Fu 8 long-range sets and a second radio operator; ammo stowage was reduced to fit the radios) that has ALSO been issued the battalion's Enigma after the staff radio truck was destroyed in the Kessel — historically wrong that it's used for platoon traffic, but every individual ingredient is real. (b) The stronger move a history-literate player will actively enjoy: DON'T claim the Enigma talks to your own platoon at all in-fiction — frame the interface as the player sitting in the commander's seat of that orphaned command Tiger, where the Funker station (Enigma + Morse key + Fu 8) is the ONLY surviving link because Soviet radio-intercept companies in the Stalingrad pocket are direction-finding and jamming voice nets ("Funkstille befohlen" — voice radio silence ordered). Your two friendly Tigers have working receivers but keep transmissions to enciphered Morse bursts to stay alive. This turns the historical WEAKNESS of Enigma (slow, deliberate, needs a Morse pass) into the game mechanic: orders take time to encipher and send, replies arrive as lamp-by-lamp decrypts — latency and terseness become tactical texture rather than an anachronism to apologize for. Sell it in one line of flavor text: "Ivan's Peilstationen triangulate every voice transmission in the Kessel. We speak only in five-letter groups now." (c) Interface honesty that buys enormous credibility: show the Enigma as it was — lamps light one at a time, no printing, no direct transmit; pair it visually with a Morse key and the Fu-set boxes on the hull wall, and let the send animation be the keyed Morse burst, not the Enigma itself 'sending'. Keep the player's typing as the encipher step. The one liberty you keep silently is compression of real 10-30 minute encode/transmit/decode cycles down to gameplay seconds — nobody will begrudge that.
procedure_flavor: Hier Anton — this is Anton (spelling-alphabet callsign: Anton, Berta, Cäsar, Dora, Emil, Friedrich)
Feindpanzer von links / rechts / vorne — enemy tanks from left/right/front
Richtung zwei Uhr — direction two o'clock
Sammeln am Sammelpunkt — rally at rally point
X = Stop/space in Enigma text; CH written as Q; numbers spelled out (acht-null-null)
